method: Model the cake as a prism with a flat top and vertical sides: a round cake as a cylinder with side area pi times diameter times height plus top area pi times diameter squared over four, a square cake as four times the side length times height plus the side length squared, and a rectangular sheet cake as twice the length plus width times height plus length times width. The base, filling layers and board are excluded. Frosted area is multiplied by the finish-coat thickness converted from millimetres to centimetres to give the finish-coat volume in millilitres, because one cubic centimetre is one millilitre. An optional crumb coat adds a second layer of 2 mm over the same area. Total volume is converted to weight at a density of 1.05 grams per millilitre and to US cups at 236.5882365 millilitres per cup. Dimensions are decimal centimetres and thickness decimal millimetres, accepted with a decimal point or comma; blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. The model assumes sharp edges and one identically frosted tier, and excludes piping, borders, filling, levelling trims and bowl losses.

sources.title: Standard geometry of a cylinder and a rectangular prism: lateral area plus one end area gives the frosted surface of a single-tier cake.
Cake-decorating practice: a crumb coat is a thin sealing layer applied before the finish coat, typically about 2 mm over the same surface.
US customary volume definition: one US cup is 236.5882365 millilitres, and icing density is around 1.05 grams per millilitre for American buttercream.
